title: Pharmacology Basics
summary: Learn how medicines work: names and regulation, pharmacokinetics and half-life, pharmacodynamics, major medicine groups and antimicrobial resistance, safe dose calculations and adverse effects. Educational only.
audience: Nursing, pharmacy and health-science students, care workers and health-curious learners

lessons.title: Medicines, names and how they are regulated

body.p: Pharmacology is the study of how medicines (drugs) act on the body and how the body handles them. Medicines prevent, diagnose, treat or relieve disease. Every medicine can cause harm as well as benefit, so the aim is always the best balance for the patient.

list: Generic (non-proprietary) name: the international name of the active ingredient, such as paracetamol (called acetaminophen in North America) or amoxicillin.
Brand name: the manufacturer's trade name. One generic medicine can have many brands.
Prescribing and learning generic names avoids confusion and supports cheaper equivalent products.

body.p: National medicines regulators, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria, SAHPRA in South Africa, the Pharmacy and Poisons Board in Kenya and the Ghana FDA, approve medicines for quality, safety and effectiveness, and classify them as over-the-counter, pharmacy-only or prescription medicines. Falsified and substandard medicines are a serious problem in many countries; buy only from licensed pharmacies and outlets.

body.tip: This course is educational. Always follow the advice of a prescriber or pharmacist, and the official product information, for any real medicine use.

lessons.title: Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to drugs

body.p: Pharmacokinetics describes four processes, often remembered as ADME:

list: Absorption: how the drug enters the bloodstream. Oral drugs pass through the gut and liver first (first-pass metabolism), so some are inactivated; intravenous drugs are fully available immediately.
Distribution: how the drug spreads to tissues, affected by blood flow, binding to proteins and barriers such as the blood-brain barrier.
Metabolism: mainly in the liver, changing drugs into forms that are easier to excrete; liver disease and some interacting drugs alter it.
Excretion: mainly through the kidneys in urine; reduced kidney function can cause drugs to build up.

body.p: The half-life is the time for the drug's concentration in the blood to fall by half. A drug with a half-life of 6 hours, starting at an amount of 200 mg in the body, falls to 100, 50, 25 and then 12.5 mg after 24 hours (four half-lives). With regular dosing, a drug reaches steady state after about 4 to 5 half-lives; after 5 half-lives about 97% of a single dose has been eliminated.

body.tip: Half-life explains why some medicines are taken once a day and others several times a day.

lessons.title: Pharmacodynamics: what drugs do to the body

body.p: Pharmacodynamics describes how drugs produce their effects. Most act on targets such as receptors, enzymes or ion channels.

list: Agonists activate receptors (for example salbutamol opens the airways by stimulating beta-2 receptors).
Antagonists block receptors (for example beta-blockers slow the heart by blocking beta-1 receptors).
Enzyme inhibitors block enzymes (for example ACE inhibitors reduce blood pressure).
Antimicrobials target structures in microbes that human cells lack, such as bacterial cell walls.

body.p: Effects increase with dose up to a maximum. The therapeutic window is the range between the dose that works and the dose that causes unacceptable toxicity. Drugs with a narrow window, such as warfarin, digoxin and some anti-epileptics, need careful monitoring and blood tests. Children, older people, pregnant women and people with liver or kidney disease may respond differently.

body.tip: Ask "what is this medicine for, how will we know it is working, and what side effects should we watch for?" for every medicine a patient takes.

lessons.title: Major medicine groups and antimicrobial resistance

body.p: Medicines are grouped by their use or mechanism. Some major groups:

list: Analgesics: paracetamol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, and opioids for severe pain.
Antibiotics: for bacterial infections; they do not work against viruses such as colds and flu.
Antimalarials, antiretrovirals (for HIV) and anti-tuberculosis medicines, central to public health in many countries.
Cardiovascular medicines: antihypertensives, statins and anticoagulants.
Medicines for diabetes, such as metformin and insulin.
Vaccines, which prevent rather than treat disease.

body.p: Bacteria and other microbes evolve to survive medicines, especially when antibiotics are overused, used for viral illnesses, bought without prescription or stopped early. Resistant infections are harder and more expensive to treat and cause many deaths worldwide. Prescribe and use antibiotics only when needed, at the right dose and duration, and never share them.

body.tip: Hand hygiene and vaccination reduce infections, and therefore the need for antibiotics in the first place.

body.p: Accurate calculations prevent serious errors. Always check units, write calculations down, and have high-risk calculations independently double-checked. The examples below were verified in code; real orders must follow the prescription and local protocols.

list: Tablets: dose ordered / strength per tablet. 500 mg ordered with 250 mg tablets: 500 / 250 = 2 tablets.
Liquids: (dose ordered / stock strength) x volume. 375 mg ordered from a 250 mg in 5 mL suspension: 375 / 250 x 5 = 7.5 mL.
Weight-based doses: dose per kg x weight. 10 mg/kg for an 18 kg child = 180 mg (check against the maximum dose).
Infusion rate: volume / time. 1000 mL over 8 hours = 125 mL per hour.
Drip rate with a giving set of 20 drops per mL: 125 x 20 / 60, about 41.7, rounded to 42 drops per minute.
1 g = 1000 mg; 1 mg = 1000 micrograms. Confusing mg and micrograms causes thousand-fold errors.
Write "units" in full rather than "U", which can be misread as 0.
Never use a trailing zero (5.0 mg can be misread as 50 mg); always use a leading zero (0.5 mg).

body.tip: If a calculated dose seems unusual, such as many tablets or a very large volume, stop and recheck before giving it.

lessons.title: Side effects, interactions and safe use

body.p: An adverse drug reaction is an unwanted, harmful effect. Some are predictable from the drug's actions (for example drowsiness or stomach upset); others are unpredictable, such as allergic reactions, which can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis).

list: Drug-drug: one drug changes the effect of another, for example some antibiotics and anti-tuberculosis drugs change levels of other medicines.
Drug-food: alcohol increases sedation; some foods affect absorption.
Drug-herb: traditional and herbal remedies can interact with prescribed medicines; always ask patients what else they take.
Drug-disease: NSAIDs can worsen kidney disease and stomach ulcers.

body.p: Pharmacovigilance is monitoring medicine safety after approval. Health workers and patients should report suspected adverse reactions to the national regulator; these reports reveal rare problems that clinical trials missed.

body.tip: Record allergies clearly, including what happened, and check them before every new medicine.
